1.pericope_label: Unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul: shew me thy ways: remember not the sins of my youth

schools.summary: Augustine hears Christ speaking in the person of the Church, so that the psalm belongs to the Christian people turned to God, reads the shame of the second verse as the shame of one who wished to be as God and then feared death from the smallest insect, and takes the mocking enemies for those who ensnare by secret suggestion and flatter the soul with Well done.

Gill offers three senses for lifting up the soul, in prayer on the authority of the Chaldee, as an offering, or as a deposit committed to God for safe keeping, and refuses to treat the sins of youth as mere inadvertence, reading the plea as a confession of sinning from youth upward; Calvin takes the psalm for meditations mingled with prayers in which David owns that God has justly chastised him, and rejects outright the reading that makes the opening a self-offering in sacrifice.

Henry makes prayer the ascent of the soul to God and recalls the ancient call to devotion, Up with your hearts; Spurgeon allows that the soul is often more like a burrowing mole than a soaring eagle and holds that faith must be the lever and grace the arm until the loadstone of the Saviour’s love does the lifting.

Clarke counts the defects in the acrostic, two letters missing and one doubled and a line left over, and turns them into an indictment of the care with which the Hebrew Scriptures were preserved, before supplying four manuscripts and six versions that restore the missing letter; he places the psalm among the captives in Babylon, and distinguishes the two words of the sixth verse as the commiseration felt in the bowels and the kindnesses born of a profusion of benevolence. Wesley glosses being ashamed as being disappointed of hope.

Ellicott corrects the English twice, waiting on God being waiting for him from a root meaning to make strong by twisting, and the received version wrongly following a Greek imperative where the line is a promise rather than a wish; Keil and Delitzsch class the psalm among nine alphabetical psalms and pair it with a companion that lacks the same letter and adds the same extra strophe, inferring one common author, find no historical background or individuality in it at all, and observe that the written word still needs God himself as its expounder.

debates: Is the missing letter a defect or a design? Clarke counts two letters absent, one doubled in place of a third and a line standing outside the series, calls the psalm proof that the Hebrew Scriptures were carelessly kept, and restores the letter from four collated manuscripts and six versions; Keil and Delitzsch treat the same absence as original, since a companion alphabetical psalm lacks the very same letter, matches this one at three strophes and adds the same supernumerary strophe at the end, which they take as evidence of one common author.

Has the psalm a historical setting? Clarke refers it to the captives in Babylon and reads those who deal treacherously as idolaters, putting a complaint against the Chaldeans into the speaker’s mouth; Keil and Delitzsch say it has no definite background indicating the history of the times and no clearly marked traits of individuality, and read it as an answer to the question the preceding psalm had raised; Augustine assigns it to Christ speaking in the person of the Church.

What is it to lift up the soul? Gill allows three senses, prayer on the authority of the Chaldee, an offering presented as a living sacrifice, and a deposit committed to God for keeping; Calvin names the second and rejects it, saying that those who imagine David declares he had offered himself in sacrifice do not properly understand the passage, the point being rather that he does not gaze about for help from the world as the ungodly do.
outliers: Clarke uses a defective acrostic as an occasion to attack the reputation of the Jewish scribes, saying it is fashionable to be violent in praise of their fidelity and that such praise is in general ill placed, and then repairs the defect himself from manuscripts and versions.

Ellicott holds the Authorised Version in error for following an imperative found in the Greek, so that a promise that none who wait for God shall be ashamed has been turned into a wish that they may not be.

Keil and Delitzsch close their comment on the seventh verse by quoting Augustine’s own prayer that God would remember him not according to the anger he deserves but according to the mercy that is worthy of God, a father whose exposition of this psalm stands beside theirs.
Keil and Delitzsch concede that the will of God lies before us in the written word while insisting that the expounder required for the right understanding of that word is God himself.
themes: a letter missing from two psalms at once
praise for scribes withdrawn over one broken line
a promise mistaken for a wish
a soul lifted, offered, or deposited
mercy named from the bowels and from abundance

8.pericope_label: Good and upright is the Lord: all the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth: the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him

schools.summary: Henry notes that the petition for pardon comes in abruptly and belongs earlier, finds the reason given surprising and turns it into a rule that confession must aggravate sin, takes the paths for the promises and providences together, and declines to decide whose choice is meant since it comes all to one; Spurgeon calls the plea the logic of faith against a legal spirit, holds that pardoning a great sinner brings great glory, and says God does not violate the will but instructs it.

Gill presses the word for meek toward the miserable and afflicted who ask what they must do to be saved and are led on gently by degrees, cites an interpreter for the sin with Bathsheba behind the plea for pardon while also allowing the sin of his nature, and takes the secret for the secret of God’s purposes and of his providences.

Clarke derives the paths from the ruts wagon wheels leave in ground often crossed, makes the meek the poor and distressed whose cause God brings to a happy issue, prefers the marginal lodging in goodness to the text, and reads the secret as a secret assembly, many who fear God having a church in their own house; Wesley reads the particle in the plea for pardon as though rather than because, notes that the word means both great and much, glosses the way as the one God appoints, and calls the secret God’s love and favour, known only to the one who enjoys it.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that one word carries both gentleness and lowliness and that Jerome renders it two ways in one verse, prefer the way the man should choose against the Greek referring it to God, take the verb of lodging as tarrying the night, and derive the secret from a pressing close together for confidential converse; Ellicott renders the pair grace and truth and hears the conception of God passing from Law to Gospel, gives the same rendering of the choice while recording that the versions differ, and derives the secret from a couch and the talk of those who sit on it.

debates: Why should a great sin be pardoned? Henry and Spurgeon both read the clause as a reason, the greatness of the sin being the argument, since the glory of forgiveness rises with what is forgiven; Wesley refuses the reading, holding that the particle is often rendered though, so that the prayer is that the sin be pardoned although it is great, and adds that the word means much as well as great, which would make the plea one of number rather than weight.

Whose choice is meant in the way that he shall choose? Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both refer it to the man, the way of right choice, and both record that the Greek and the Latin refer it instead to God as the way in which he takes delight; Wesley follows the versions and glosses it as the way God appoints; Clarke takes it of the calling Providence has chosen for a man; Henry refuses to decide, on the ground that one who fears God chooses what pleases God.

What is the secret of the Lord? Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott independently derive it from sitting close together for confidential talk, Ellicott from a couch and the conversation of those on it, and Keil and Delitzsch noting that the Greek took the word for strength as though from a different root; Clarke makes it a secret assembly and thinks of a church in a private house; Gill makes it the secret of the divine purposes and providences; Wesley makes it a favour known only to the one enjoying it.
outliers: Henry observes that the petition for pardon comes in abruptly where it stands and should have followed the seventh verse, a displacement noticed independently of the psalm’s broken alphabet.
Clarke derives the paths of the Lord from cart ruts worn into ground crossed again and again, so that mercy and truth can be tracked by the depth of the marks they leave.

Ellicott offers the English word board as a direct analogy for a word that moved from a piece of furniture to the conversation held at it, and notes that a borrowed word for a couch has travelled the same road in the opposite direction.
Keil and Delitzsch hold that God would have to force himself upon the self-righteous against their will, and that what he wants is disciples eager to learn.
themes: a sin pleaded by its own size
one particle read as because and as though
mercy tracked by the ruts it leaves
a secret named from the couch it is told on
a will instructed rather than overruled

15.pericope_label: Mine eyes are ever toward the Lord: turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me, for I am desolate and afflicted

schools.summary: Henry makes the solitude deliberate, David relying as entirely on God as if no creature could help, notes that the psalmist asks no more for his affliction than that God look on it while asking no less for his sin than full pardon, and contrasts an eye of faith with idolaters who wanted gods their bodily eyes could see; Spurgeon holds that unbelief suggests God has turned his back, that the quarrel is always on our side, that saints never get beyond the publican’s prayer, and that one who trod the winepress alone can succour the solitary.

Gill keeps the received division of the seventeenth verse while offering a second sense from it, that troubles have enlarged the heart and increased a man’s knowledge and experience, and supplies the history behind the affliction and the pain, the rebellion of his own subjects under his son and either the uneasiness of mind or the fatigue of flight.

Clarke marks the verse that should have carried the missing letter and the letter that stands twice instead, reports two conjectural restorations and concedes that every version already read the present text, and keeps his thesis that these are the words of the captives in Babylon, whose evils seem to multiply rather than lessen; Wesley reduces the plucking of the feet to deliverance out of all troubles.

Keil and Delitzsch hold the missing letter compensated by a doubled strophe of the next and note the Greek imperative standing twice, but suspect the received division of the words in the preceding verse and redivide it so that God is asked to enlarge the straits of the heart; they fix the word for desolate as one who has no companion, observe an undisguised chime of similar sounds, and find it pleasing that no vengeance is invoked. Ellicott reports the consensus of commentators for the same redivision.

debates: Should the missing letter be restored? Clarke marks the verse that ought to carry it, notes that its neighbour stands twice, reports two conjectural words offered by scholars, and admits that the loss is old enough for every version to have read the present text; Keil and Delitzsch treat the loss as compensated by a doubled strophe of the following letter and observe that the Greek repeats the imperative, so that nothing needs restoring.

How should the seventeenth verse be divided? Keil and Delitzsch call the received division a poor antithesis and hold the original text undoubtedly divided the consonants otherwise, so that God is asked to enlarge the straits of the heart; Ellicott reports the consensus of commentators for the same change; Gill keeps the received words and offers instead a second sense within them, that troubles have enlarged the heart by increasing knowledge and experience.
outliers: The two parties change sides between the two verses: the commentators who refused to mend the broken acrostic are the ones who redivide the consonants of the line before it, while the commentator who wanted the acrostic repaired leaves that line exactly as he found it.

Keil and Delitzsch find it pleasing to a New Testament conscience that the psalm nowhere expressly invokes vengeance upon the enemies, even while defining their hatred as one that springs from injustice and ends in injustice.
Henry observes that the psalmist asks no more for his affliction than that God look upon it and do as he pleases, but asks no less for his sin than that all of it be forgiven.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the psalm makes no attempt to avoid the chime of two words that sound alike in the verse about desolation.
themes: a letter lost or a letter compensated
consonants divided two ways
solitude chosen rather than suffered
an affliction submitted and a sin pressed
a hatred that begins and ends in injustice

19.pericope_label: Consider mine enemies, for they are many: let integrity and uprightness preserve me: redeem Israel, O God

schools.summary: Gill asks for a look of another kind upon the enemies, such as God gave the Egyptians through the pillar of fire, notes that the plea draws on both their number and their nature, leaves the integrity of the twenty-first verse open between the psalmist’s own innocence, a prayer that it be preserved in him, and the faithfulness of God, and reads the closing prayer of a nation caught in a rebellion and beyond that of redemption by the Messiah.

Clarke agrees that the closing verse stands outside the alphabetical arrangement and takes it for a general prayer for redemption from captivity, observes that the people had been prayed for as one person until the psalmist widened his heart to take in his fellow sufferers, reduces the integrity of the twenty-first verse to a wish for a perfect heart and an upright life, and notes that the psalm ends where it began; Wesley turns the last verse into an offer, that if God will not help him he may yet spare a people suffering for his sake.

Ellicott judges the closing line a later addition, isolated, interfering with the alphabet and using a different name for God; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict independently, suspect it was added when the psalm entered public worship, and speculate that the supernumerary strophes here and in the companion psalm may answer to two Greek letters or to a habit of representing the final letters at the close of synagogue hymns. They also personify the two virtues of the twenty-first verse as guardians on a road made dangerous by the traveller’s own sinfulness, and ground the plea against shame in the hope resting on God himself.

debates: Is the last verse part of the psalm? Ellicott calls it apparently a later addition, isolated, interfering with the alphabetical arrangement and using a different divine name from the rest; Keil and Delitzsch independently judge that it looks to have been added when the psalm came into public worship and cite the same change of name; Clarke agrees that it stands out of the order and did not form part of the alphabetical arrangement. Three commentators, two of them resting on the same evidence.

Whose integrity is to preserve him? Gill offers three readings without deciding, the psalmist’s own innocence as a ruler rebelled against without cause, a prayer that integrity and uprightness be kept in him against his own corruptions and his rebels’ provocations, or the integrity and uprightness of God, meaning his goodness and covenant faithfulness; Clarke takes it simply as a wish for a perfect heart and an upright life; Keil and Delitzsch make the two virtues guardians travelling with him.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch, having found supernumerary strophes at the end of this psalm and of its companion, wonder whether the two extra letters answer to two Greek letters of similar sound, or whether both are instances of a habit of representing the final letters specially, as is sometimes done at the close of synagogue hymns.
Wesley reads the closing intercession as a bargain offered in extremity: if God will not help the speaker, he may yet spare a people who suffer for the speaker’s sake and in his sufferings.

Clarke observes that the people had been prayed for through the preceding verses as though they were a single person, and that the psalmist widens the prayer at the end lest his own necessities narrow his heart and make him forget his fellow sufferers.

Keil and Delitzsch turn the private prayer into a principle, that the enmity of the world and of sin brings all God’s people into the same straits, so that the need of one will not cease until the need of the whole has a radical remedy.
themes: a verse outside its own alphabet
a divine name that changes in one line
integrity claimed, asked for, or ascribed to God
a look of a different kind
a prayer that widens at the last moment
